title: Traffic 101
summary: What traffic is, where it comes from and why some people are far more likely to act than others. You will learn how the ad auction sets your price and how to pick a first traffic source that fits a small budget.

lessons.title: What traffic is
objectives: By the end you can explain what you are actually buying when you buy traffic.
You can tell paid, owned and earned traffic apart.
You can judge traffic by cost per result instead of cost per click.

steps.p: Traffic means people arriving at your ad, page or channel. When you buy traffic, you buy a chance to be seen by a person. Their interest, trust and money still have to be earned by your offer and your message.
steps.more: New buyers often talk about traffic as if it were a product with fixed quality, like buying rice by the bag. It is closer to renting a stall in a busy market. The platform puts you in front of people, but whether anyone stops, listens and buys depends on who those people are and what you show them. That is why two buyers on the same platform, with the same budget, can get completely different results.
steps.say: Let's start with what traffic really is. Traffic means people arriving at your ad, your page or your channel. When you buy traffic, you buy a chance to be seen by a person. That's all. Their interest, their trust and their money still have to be earned by your offer and your message. Think of it like renting a stall in a busy market. The platform puts you in front of people, but whether anyone stops depends on who they are and what you show them.

steps.h: The units you buy and sell
steps.p: Traffic is sold in units, and each step down this line is worth more than the one before. You usually buy near the top, as impressions or clicks, and get paid near the bottom, for a lead or a deposit. The gap between them is your job.
steps.more: An impression is one showing of your ad on a screen. A click is a person tapping it. A lead is a person giving their details. A deposit or sale is a person paying. If you pay per impression, you carry the risk that nobody clicks. If you pay per click, the platform carries part of that risk, but you still carry the risk that clickers never sign up. Either way, the advertiser only pays you at the bottom. Your skill is turning cheap units at the top into valuable units at the bottom.

steps.p: Traffic comes from three places. Most affiliates start with paid traffic, then build owned audiences so they are not renting every single visitor forever. Earned traffic is welcome but hard to plan around.
d: Paid|you pay per view, click or post
Earned|shares, word of mouth, search rankings
steps.say: Traffic comes from three places. Look at the cards. Paid, where you pay per view, click or post. Owned, meaning your own channel, list or website. And earned, which is shares, word of mouth and search rankings. Most affiliates start with paid traffic, then build owned audiences, so they're not renting every single visitor forever. Earned traffic is welcome, but it's hard to plan around.

steps.p: Ten thousand cheap clicks from people who will never deposit are worth less than fifty from people who might. Traffic quality is how likely the people you buy are to take the action you are paid for. Cheap traffic often turns out to be expensive per result.
steps.say: Here's a rule you'll use every day: judge cost per result. Ten thousand cheap clicks from people who will never deposit are worth less than fifty clicks from people who might. Traffic quality is how likely the people you buy are to take the action you're paid for. And cheap traffic often turns out to be expensive per result. Cheap clicks can be costly.

steps.p: Example: Source A sells clicks at $0.02 and Source B at $0.25. You spend $100 on each. A brings 5,000 clicks and 1 deposit. B brings 400 clicks and 4 deposits. On a $40 payout, A loses $60 and B earns $60.
steps.more: Work it through. Source A: $100 buys 5,000 clicks. 1 deposit × $40 = $40 returned, a $60 loss. Its cost per deposit is $100. Source B: $100 buys 400 clicks. 4 deposits × $40 = $160 returned, a $60 profit. Its cost per deposit is $25. Source A looked twelve times cheaper per click and was four times more expensive per deposit. The numbers are an example, but the lesson holds everywhere: price per click tells you very little until you know how many of those clicks become results.

d.text: A: $100 for 1 FTD = $100 per FTD. B: $100 for 4 FTDs = $25 per FTD. The cheap clicks were the expensive ones.

steps.h: Signs of good and bad traffic
steps.p: You will not see quality directly. You see it in behaviour. Look for these signs in your tracker and the network's dashboard during your first days on any source, and pause anything that shows several warning signs together.

a.title: Good signs
items: People spend time on your page
Deposits come from the right geo

b.title: Warning signs
items: Clicks with almost no time on page

steps.say: You won't see quality directly. You see it in behaviour. On the left, good signs: people spend time on your page, sign-ups verify their email or phone, deposits come from the right geo, and some users come back. On the right, warning signs: clicks with almost no time on page, many sign-ups but zero deposits, users from unlisted countries, and sudden spikes at odd hours. Watch for these in your first days on any source, and pause anything that shows several warning signs together.

steps.h: Not every click is a person
steps.p: Some traffic is fake: bots, click farms and accidental taps. Large platforms filter much of it, while smaller ad networks vary widely. Fake traffic wastes your money and can get your conversions rejected by the advertiser. Judge traffic by real actions.
steps.more: A bot is software that loads pages and clicks links like a person would. A click farm is a group of people or devices paid to click or install. Some low-quality sites also place ads where people tap them by mistake. Advertisers watch for this because it brings them sign-ups that never deposit, and networks reject conversions they believe are fraudulent. You protect yourself by buying from reputable sources, checking behaviour rather than click counts, and blocking placements that send clicks without actions.

And some sites place ads where people tap them by mistake. Large platforms filter much of this, while smaller ad networks vary widely. Fake traffic wastes your money, and it can get your conversions rejected by the advertiser. As the screen says, bots click, people deposit. Judge traffic by real actions.

steps.p: Each type reaches people in a different state of mind, which shapes the kind of ad and page that works. The next lesson takes each source in turn. For now, notice how differently people arrive from each one.
steps.say: Here are the main traffic types at a glance. Look at the last column, the user's state of mind. On search, they're looking for something. On social, they're scrolling and relaxed. On native, they're reading. Push and pops interrupt them, and pops often annoy them. With influencers, they trust the creator. And on Telegram, they're reading a feed they chose. Each state shapes what kind of ad and page works. The next lesson takes each source in turn.

steps.p: Every traffic decision comes back to one comparison: what it costs you to get a result against what that result pays you. If the left side is lower, you have something to grow. If it is higher, you have a lesson to learn cheaply.
steps.say: Every traffic decision comes back to this one comparison. Your cost per result must be below your payout per result. If the left side is lower, you have something to grow. If it's higher, you have a lesson to learn, and the goal is to learn it cheaply. Keep this line in your head every time you look at a dashboard.

steps.h: Rent attention, then own some of it
steps.p: Paid traffic is rented: when you stop paying, it stops. Owned audiences, such as a Telegram channel or an email list people chose to join, let you reach people again without paying for each view. Strong operators use paid traffic to grow owned audiences.
steps.more: Owned audiences must be built with consent. People should know what they are joining and be able to leave easily. Buying lists, adding people to groups without asking or messaging people who did not opt in breaks platform rules and, in many countries, data protection law. Done honestly, an owned audience lowers your cost per result over time, because each new message reaches people you already paid to meet once.

d.s: Build lists people chose to join

steps.say: Paid traffic is rented. When you stop paying, it stops. Owned audiences, like a Telegram channel or an email list people chose to join, let you reach people again without paying for each view. Strong operators use paid traffic to grow owned audiences. But it must be built with consent. People should know what they're joining and be able to leave easily. Buying lists or adding people without asking breaks platform rules, and in many countries, data protection law.

steps.p: Here is the rent-then-own idea as a system. Paid ads bring people once. Some of them choose to join your channel. From then on you can reach them again with posts that cost nothing per view, and some go on to the offer later.
steps.say: Here's rent, then own, as a map. Follow the arrows. A paid ad brings a paid click to your page. From there, some people go straight to the offer. Others choose to join your Telegram channel. They read your free posts, and some click through to the offer later. Approved sign-ups lead to your payout. The key idea is that paid ads bring people once, and your channel lets you reach them again, at no cost per view.

steps.p: Answer these five questions before you spend a single dollar on any source. If you cannot answer one, stop and find out. Each gap is a common way beginners lose their first budget without learning anything useful.
d: What is my payout per result?
Which unit am I paying for?
How will I count real results?
What is my maximum test spend?
Does the offer allow this source?

steps.h: Common traffic mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: New buyers lose most of their first budget to a handful of mistakes about traffic. Each fix below is free. The hard part is remembering them when a cheap click price looks tempting.
d: Judging by CPC|judge by cost per result
Buying the cheapest source|cheap clicks are often bots
Adding people without consent|owned audiences must opt in
No tracking before spend|count real results first
Ignoring the offer's traffic rules|banned sources get scrubbed
steps.say: New buyers lose most of their first budget to a handful of mistakes. Judging by C P C, cost per click, instead of cost per result. Buying the cheapest source, when cheap clicks are often bots. Adding people without consent, when owned audiences must opt in. No tracking before spend, when you need to count real results first. And ignoring the offer's traffic rules, because banned sources get scrubbed. Each fix is free. The hard part is remembering them when a cheap click looks tempting.

steps.h: Never buy fake or forced attention
steps.p: Buying bots, paying people to click or join, adding people to groups without asking and messaging people who never opted in all break platform rules, and in many countries data protection law. Advertisers also reject the results. There is no safe version of these.

d.text: Real people, real consent, real interest. Anything else gets scrubbed, banned or both.

steps.say: This is an important warning. Buying bots, paying people to click or join, adding people to groups without asking, and messaging people who never opted in, all break platform rules, and in many countries, data protection law. Advertisers also reject the results. There's no safe version of any of these. As the screen says, real people, real consent, real interest. Anything else gets scrubbed, banned, or both.

takeaways: Buying traffic buys a chance to be seen. Interest and trust are earned by the offer and the message.
Judge traffic by cost per result. Cheap clicks are often the most expensive per deposit.
Use paid traffic to build owned audiences, with consent, so you reach people again without paying every time.

lessons.title: The main traffic sources
objectives: By the end you can name the main traffic sources and what each one is good for.
You can list the main risks and policy limits of each source.
You can ask the right questions before testing any new source.

steps.p: Each traffic source is a different door into people's attention. They differ in who is there, what mood people are in, how you target them, what they allow and what they cost. This lesson is a tour. Later modules go deep on the ones you will use most.

d.s: Learn what each door is good for

steps.say: Each traffic source is a different door into people's attention. As the screen says, same goal, different doors. They differ in who is there, what mood people are in, how you target them, what they allow, and what they cost. This lesson is a tour, so you know what each door is good for. Later modules go deep on the ones you'll use most.

steps.p: These are the main groups you will hear about. Platform features, policies and country availability change often, so treat any specific detail in this lesson as something to check in the platform's current help pages before you plan a campaign.
d: Push and pops|notifications and new windows
Telegram and SEO|channels and organic search
steps.say: Here's the map of sources. Paid social, like Meta, TikTok and Snapchat. Search, like Google and Bing. Native, ads placed among content. Push and pops, notifications and new windows. Influencers, creators with audiences. And Telegram and S E O, channels and organic search. One important habit: platform features, policies and country availability change often. steps.p: Meta sells ads across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and partner apps. Its strengths are large reach in many countries and a delivery system that learns who converts from the data you send it. It is strict on restricted categories such as gambling, finance and health.
steps.more: When you tell Meta which action you want, such as a sign-up, and send it data each time that action happens, its delivery system looks for more people similar to those who converted. This is why tracking matters so much on Meta. Meta also reviews ads and accounts, and repeated policy breaks can restrict your account or business. At the time of writing, gambling ads need Meta's written permission, and financial products have their own policies that differ by country; check the current policy pages before relying on this. Campaign objectives, settings and button names change regularly, so check the current Ads Manager and help centre.

Its strengths are huge reach in many countries, and a delivery system that learns who converts from the data you send it. That's why tracking matters so much on Meta. The catch is strict rules on restricted categories, like gambling, finance and health. At the time of writing, gambling ads need Meta's written permission, and financial products have their own policies that differ by country. Check the current policy pages before relying on this.

steps.p: TikTok and Snapchat reach many younger users through full-screen vertical video. Ads that look like normal content, such as a person talking to camera, usually fit better than polished studio ads. Both restrict or ban some financial and gambling ads in many countries.
steps.more: Self-serve ad accounts are not available in every country, and the list of countries you can target also differs from the list where you can open an account. Check both before you plan. Each platform has its own pixel and server-side event tools, its own review process and its own creative style. A video that works on Meta often needs re-editing to feel natural on TikTok. Treat each platform as a new source to learn, even when the ad formats look similar.

steps.p: Search ads appear when someone types a query. The person is already looking, which is called intent. Clicks often cost more and volume is limited to how many people search. Many affiliate offers ban bidding on the advertiser's own brand name.

a.title: Strengths
items: Clear link between query and offer

steps.say: Search ads appear when someone types a query. The person is already looking, and that's called intent. On the left, the strengths: the person is already searching, there's a clear link between the query and the offer, and it's easy to measure per keyword. On the right, the limits: clicks usually cost more, volume is capped by how many people search, brand bidding is often banned by offers, and finance and gambling rules are strict.

steps.p: Native ads look like content: a headline and image placed among articles on news and entertainment sites, bought through native ad networks. People are reading, so ads that lead to a useful article or comparison page fit best. Site quality varies a lot.
steps.more: Native traffic is bought across thousands of websites, and some send much better users than others. You learn by tracking results per site, then blocking poor ones and focusing budget on good ones. Native has a reputation problem: some advertisers use fake news pages, invented celebrity endorsements and false stories to sell products. Never do this. Pages must be labelled as advertising where required, and every claim must be true. Native also tends to need more budget to learn than social, because there are so many sites to sort through.
steps.say: Native ads look like content, a headline and image placed among articles on news and entertainment sites. People are reading, so ads that lead to a useful article or comparison page fit best. Site quality varies a lot, so you track results per site and block poor ones. And a warning: native has a reputation problem, with fake news pages and invented celebrity endorsements. Never do this. As the screen says, honest headlines only, and every claim must be true.

steps.p: Push and pop traffic is cheap per click and available in large volume. Intent is low and fake traffic can be high, so many trading and iGaming offers ban it. Treat it as an advanced source and check the offer rules before any test.

rows: Browser alerts to people who opted in

steps.say: Push and pop traffic is cheap per click and comes in large volume. Look at the table. Push sends browser alerts to people who opted in, but intent is low and opt-ins can be weak. In-page push is an alert-style banner on a site, with lots of accidental taps. Popunders open a window behind the page, and bring bots, so offers often ban them. Many trading and iGaming offers ban this traffic, so treat it as advanced, and check the offer rules before any test.

steps.p: You can pay creators to mention or review an offer to their audience. Trust can be high when the creator fits the topic. Results are hard to predict and hard to track without unique links or codes. Paid posts must be clearly marked as ads.
steps.more: Example: you pay $150 for one post. It gets 8,000 views, 40 clicks on your unique link and 2 FTDs at $40, so $80 back and a $70 loss. A second creator at the same price might bring 6 FTDs and a profit. You only find out by testing small, tracking each creator separately and repeating what works. Agree in writing what the creator will say, make sure they disclose the paid partnership as their country and platform require, and never let them claim results, profits or guarantees.
steps.say: You can pay creators to mention or review an offer to their audience. When the creator fits the topic, trust can be high. But results are hard to predict, and hard to track without unique links or codes. For example, one post for one hundred and fifty dollars might bring two F T Ds, first-time deposits, at forty dollars, a seventy dollar loss, while another creator might bring a profit. So test small, and track each one separately. And paid posts must always be clearly marked as ads.

steps.p: Telegram is a major channel in many affiliate verticals. You can buy posts in other people's channels, use Telegram's own ad platform where it is available to you (availability, minimums and rules change; check Telegram's current ad terms), or send paid social traffic into your own channel. A channel you own lets you talk to people again and again.
steps.more: Buying posts means agreeing a price with a channel owner for one or more posts. Quality varies greatly. Some channels have inflated subscriber counts or low engagement, so look at views per post and ask for results from earlier advertisers. Use a unique join link or tracking link for each channel so you can measure them separately. Running ads into your own channel is a common funnel in trading and iGaming, and it is covered in the funnels module. Telegram's terms and ad rules also apply.

d.b: Buy posts or grow your own
d.s: An owned channel gives repeat reach

steps.say: Telegram is a major channel in many affiliate verticals. steps.h: Buying a Telegram post: the chat
steps.p: Example chat with a channel owner before a post buy. The buyer asks for real view numbers, a price, a unique link and whether the channel marks paid posts. A good owner answers plainly. One who refuses to share views is telling you something too.

messages.text: Hi, I would like one post about a free betting-odds guide in my channel. What are your average views per post over the last 2 weeks?
About 6,500 views per post. 48,000 subscribers. Price $60 per post, pinned for 24 hours.
Thanks. I will use my own invite link to measure joins. Do you mark paid posts as ads? I will send the text for your approval.
Yes, we add #ad. Send the text and link and I will schedule it for tomorrow 7pm.

steps.say: Here's an example chat before buying a Telegram post. The buyer asks for average views over the last two weeks. The owner answers, about six thousand five hundred views per post, forty eight thousand subscribers, sixty dollars per post, pinned for twenty four hours. The buyer says they'll use their own invite link to measure joins, and asks if paid posts are marked as ads. The owner says yes. A good owner answers plainly. One who refuses to share views is telling you something too.

steps.h: SEO: slow to start, then steady
steps.p: SEO means search engine optimisation: earning free visits from search engines by publishing useful pages. It costs time more than cash and takes months to build. Example: paid traffic stops when spending stops, while organic traffic grows slowly and keeps coming.
steps.more: In this example, a buyer runs paid ads for four months and stops in month five, so paid visits fall to zero. Meanwhile a small site of honest guides starts with no visits and grows month by month. Real SEO results vary hugely and are never guaranteed, because search engines change how they rank pages. For most beginners, SEO is a long-term side project, run alongside paid traffic, that builds an asset you own.

steps.h: Questions to ask about any source
steps.p: Ask these before testing any new source. A single no is usually enough to rule it out for now. Write your answers down with the date you checked, because policies, minimums and country access can change from one month to the next.
d: Does my offer allow this source?
Can I target my geo here?
Can I pay with my local methods?

lessons.title: Intent versus interruption
objectives: By the end you can say whether a source brings people with intent or interrupts them.
You can explain why cold traffic needs a warm-up step and honest hooks.
You can compare two sources by cost per result even when their funnels look very different.

steps.p: People meet your ad in one of two states. With intent, they are already looking for something like your offer. With interruption, they were doing something else and your ad must earn their attention. Your ads, pages and expectations must match the state.

d.s: Match your message to the state

steps.say: People meet your ad in one of two states. With intent, they're already looking for something like your offer. With interruption, they were doing something else, and your ad has to earn their attention. As the screen asks, are they looking, or scrolling? Your ads, your pages and your expectations must match that state.

steps.h: Intent and interruption side by side
steps.p: Neither state is better. Each needs a different approach. Search is the clearest intent source. Social feeds, native and push are interruption sources. Most of the difference shows up in how many people convert and what each click costs.
steps.say: Here they are side by side. On the left, intent, like search. The person types a need. There are fewer people, but they're warmer, clicks cost more, and you need to answer their question fast. On the right, interruption, like social and native. The person is scrolling. There are many people, but they're colder, clicks cost less, and you need to stop them, then explain. Neither state is better. Each needs a different approach.

steps.h: How a cold person warms up
steps.p: An interrupted person usually starts unaware of your offer. Your ad and funnel walk them up these steps. Asking a cold person to deposit in one jump usually fails, which is why funnels add a helpful page, a short quiz or a channel in between.
steps.more: Cold traffic means people who have never heard of you or the offer. Warm traffic means people who already know something about it, such as members of your Telegram channel or people who visited your page before. A good warm-up step gives honest, useful information: how the product works, what it costs, what the risks are and what happens after sign-up. It filters out people who are not a fit and prepares the right people to act. The funnels module covers this in detail.
steps.say: An interrupted person usually starts unaware of your offer. Follow the steps: unaware, curious, interested, then ready to act. Your ad and funnel walk them up these steps. Asking a cold person to deposit in one jump usually fails. That's why funnels add a helpful page, a short quiz or a channel in between. A good warm-up step gives honest information, how it works, what it costs, and what the risks are. The funnels module covers this in detail.

steps.h: Social creates demand, search catches it
steps.p: On social platforms you create demand: the person had no plan to sign up until they saw your ad. On search you catch demand that already exists. Both can work. They need different creatives, different budgets and different amounts of patience.

On search, you catch demand that already exists. Both can work. But they need different creatives, different budgets, and different amounts of patience.

lessons.title: How the ad auction sets your price
objectives: By the end you can explain CPM, CPC and CTR and calculate one from the others.
You can explain in simple terms why a more relevant ad can win at a lower bid.
You can list the main drivers of ad costs and the honest ways to lower them.

steps.p: When a person opens a feed or runs a search, the platform runs a very fast auction to decide which ads they see. Many advertisers want that person at the same moment. Your price depends on the competition, the bids and how relevant each ad is.

d.s: Run in a fraction of a second

steps.say: Every ad slot is auctioned. When a person opens a feed or runs a search, the platform runs a very fast auction, in a fraction of a second, to decide which ads they see. Many advertisers want that same person at the same moment. So your price depends on the competition, the bids, and how relevant each ad is.

steps.p: These three numbers explain most of what happens in the auction. The numbers module covers every metric in depth. For now, learn what each means and how to calculate it from your ad dashboard.
steps.say: Here are three numbers to learn first. C P M, cost per thousand impressions, is spend divided by impressions, times one thousand. C P C, cost per click, is spend divided by clicks. And C T R, click-through rate, is clicks divided by impressions. These three explain most of what happens in the auction. The numbers module covers every metric in depth. For now, learn what each means, and how to calculate it from your dashboard.

steps.p: CPM and CTR together decide your CPC. Example: you pay $2 per 1,000 impressions and 1 in 100 people click, a 1% CTR. That is 10 clicks per 1,000 impressions, so each click costs $2 ÷ 10 = $0.20.
steps.say: C P M and C T R together decide your C P C. Example: you pay two dollars per thousand impressions, and one in a hundred people click, a one percent C T R. That's ten clicks per thousand impressions. So each click costs two dollars divided by ten, which is twenty cents. Follow the equation on screen from left to right.

steps.h: Double the CTR, halve the CPC
steps.p: Example: the same $2 CPM, but a better ad gets a 2% CTR. Now 1,000 impressions bring 20 clicks and each costs $0.10. A better ad is often the cheapest way to lower your costs, because you pay the same for impressions and get more from them.
steps.more: In practice it can be even better than this. Platforms often reward ads that people engage with by showing them more cheaply, so a strong ad can lower your CPM as well as raising your CTR. The reverse is also true: an ad people scroll past or hide can see its CPM rise. This is the main reason experienced buyers spend so much time on creatives. The creative strategy module in School 2 covers how to test them.
steps.say: Now double the C T R. Same two dollar C P M, but a better ad gets a two percent C T R. A thousand impressions now bring twenty clicks, and each costs ten cents. You paid the same for the impressions, and got more from them. In practice it can be even better, because platforms often reward ads people engage with by showing them more cheaply. That's why a better ad is often the cheapest way to lower your costs.

steps.p: These cost drivers apply on most platforms. You control some of them, such as creative and targeting, and must simply plan around others, such as season and competition. Track your own CPM by week so you know your normal range.
steps.more: Competition: when more advertisers want the same people, prices rise. Geo: richer markets usually cost more per impression than poorer ones. steps.h: Your objective tells the auction who to find
steps.p: When you choose a campaign objective and optimisation event, you tell the platform which people to look for. Optimise for clicks and you get people who click. Optimise for sign-ups or deposits, with tracking in place, and it looks for people likely to do that.
steps.more: The optimisation event is the action you ask the platform to get more of, such as a link click, a registration or a purchase-type event you map to a deposit. Optimising for deeper events needs working tracking and enough events for the system to learn from, and early results can be expensive while it learns. Many buyers start one step higher, for example optimising for sign-ups, until they have enough deposits. Objectives and event names change, so check the current Ads Manager. The tracking module explains how events are sent.

steps.h: Never game review to lower costs
steps.p: Showing reviewers one page and users another, disguising a restricted offer or opening new accounts to escape a bad history all break platform rules. They can end your account, and in regulated verticals they can break the law. Cheaper delivery comes only from better, honest ads.

steps.h: Common auction mistakes, and the fix
steps.p: Each of these tries to beat the auction instead of feeding it a better ad. The fixes all work with the system rather than against it, which is the only approach that lasts.
d: Chasing the lowest CPM|follow it down to cost per result
Optimising for clicks on a deposit offer|use the deepest event with enough volume
Raising the bid to save a weak ad|improve the ad first
Editing every few hours|give delivery time between checkpoints
New accounts to restart learning|breaks policy; fix the ad instead

takeaways: CPM is the price of attention. CTR decides how many clicks that attention becomes. Together they set your CPC.
Auctions combine your bid with how likely people are to act and ad quality, so relevant ads can win for less.
Costs rise with competition, geo, season, narrow targeting, weak creative and deeper objectives. Plan for them and track your own range.

It stays the same
It cannot be calculated

The platform prefers new advertisers
Lower bids always win
People are more likely to act on it and its quality is higher

The CPM is too low

The geo is wrong

steps.h: How much does one test need?
steps.p: A test needs enough spend to see several results before you judge it. Example: if your target cost per FTD is $25 and you want at least 3 FTDs before deciding, plan around $75 per test. This is a rough guide, not a rule.
steps.more: One or two results can happen by luck, good or bad. Three or more start to show a pattern, and more is better. That is why a test sized for zero or one expected result teaches you almost nothing. Your target cost per result should come from your payout and the margin you want. Example: a $40 payout with a $15 margin gives a $25 target. If your budget cannot cover several results at your target, choose an offer with a lower payout and cheaper results, such as CPL, to learn on first.

steps.p: Example: with $300 set aside for testing, you could run four tests of about $75 each. If one finds a winner, it may pay for the others over time. If none do, you have bought four lessons. Never test with money you need for rent or food.
steps.more: Your bankroll is the money you can afford to lose while learning. Decide it before you start and keep it separate from your living money. Before each test, write a kill rule: the point at which you stop it. Example: stop any ad set that spends $50, which is twice the $25 target, with zero FTDs. Writing it first stops hope and frustration from making the decision for you. The Budget and kill rules module turns this into a full set of starting rules for kill, hold and scale.

Only the CPM
That your friends use Facebook

exam.q: Source A: $100 spend, 4,000 clicks, 1 FTD. Source B: $100 spend, 350 clicks, 5 FTDs. Payout is $35. What should you do?
options: Scale A, because its clicks are cheaper
Pause A and keep testing B, which has a $20 cost per FTD against A's $100
Split budget evenly, since both spent $100
Pause both, because the samples are equal
exam.why: B costs $20 per FTD on a $35 payout, while A costs $100. Cost per result decides, not cost per click.

exam.q: Your CPM is $4 and your CTR is 0.8%. A new ad lifts CTR to 1.6% at the same CPM. What are the old and new CPCs?
exam.why: 0.8% of 1,000 = 8 clicks, $4 ÷ 8 = $0.50. At 1.6%, 16 clicks, $4 ÷ 16 = $0.25. Doubling CTR halves CPC.

exam.q: You run a trading offer that bans popunder traffic. A push and pop network offers you clicks at $0.005. What do you do?
options: Test it with $20 to see what happens
Use it but send users through a different link
Use it only at night
Do not use it, because the offer bans it and conversions would likely be rejected
exam.why: Using a banned source risks rejected conversions and losing the offer. Cheap clicks do not change the offer terms.

exam.q: Payout $40, target $25 per FTD. An ad set has spent $80 with 2 network-confirmed FTDs. What do the starting rules say?
options: Scale, because it has conversions
Hold, because it has 2 FTDs
Kill: spend is past 3 × target ($75) and CPA $40 is above the $37.50 kill line
Kill, because 2 FTDs is below 3
exam.why: CPA is $80 ÷ 2 = $40. From $75 spend, the CPA kill line is the lower of 1.5 × $25 = $37.50 and the $40 break-even, so $37.50. $40 is above it.

exam.q: A campaign optimised for link clicks has a $0.04 CPC and zero sign-ups after $60. Tracking works. What is the most sensible change?
options: Lower the bid to get even cheaper clicks
Change the optimisation event to sign-ups (or the deepest event with enough volume) and check message match
Add more countries to the targeting
Ask the network to pay per click
exam.why: The platform found clickers because you asked for clicks. Optimising for a deeper event and fixing message match targets people who act.

exam.q: Ad A bids $12 with an estimated 1% action rate. Ad B bids $7 with an estimated 2% action rate. Using the simple auction model, ignoring quality, which wins?
options: A, because its bid is higher
Neither, it is a tie
It depends only on the CPM
exam.why: In the simplified model, bid × chance of action decides. B's score is higher despite the lower bid.

exam.q: You have a $200 bankroll, a $40 payout and a $28 target cost per FTD. You want at least 3 FTDs per test. How many full tests can you afford?
options: 2 tests
7 tests
5 tests
1 test
exam.why: One test is $28 × 3 = $84. $200 ÷ $84 is about 2.4, so two full tests. Consider a cheaper offer or more bankroll to learn more.

exam.q: A Telegram channel with 80,000 subscribers asks $200 per post, but its recent posts average 900 views. What is the best response?
options: Buy immediately, 80,000 is a large audience
Ask for a discount and run it with your normal link
Buy three posts to be safe
Treat the low views as a warning sign; if you test, pay little and use a unique tracking link
exam.why: Views per post show real reach. A gap that big suggests inactive or inflated subscribers, so test small and measure separately.

exam.q: Your Meta ad for a betting offer is rejected. A friend suggests showing a cooking video in the ad and redirecting clickers to the sportsbook. What do you do?
options: Do it once to test
Refuse, because it is cloaking and risks a permanent ban; check whether you have Meta's gambling permission and appeal properly
Do it but on a new account
Do it only in small countries
exam.why: Showing reviewers one thing and users another is cloaking, which breaks policy. Gambling ads need permission and must follow local law.

exam.q: Payout $50, target $30. After two weeks on Meta your cost per FTD has fallen from $70 to $40. What does the plan from this module suggest?
options: Switch to TikTok, since Meta has not worked
Stop testing, since you are above target
Stay within your bankroll and rule card: $40 is under the $45 kill line, so keep testing hooks and audiences and review at 30 days
Double the budget to reach $30 faster
exam.why: The CPA kill line is the lower of 1.5 × $30 = $45 and the $50 break-even, so $45. At $40 the trend is good and the rules say hold, not scale. Give the source its planned month.
